reason: Rhizophores can be thread-like. 'liliformes' is a typo of 'filiformes'.
Young shoots can be velvety. Some examples say 'velue' (hairy), which is a different term.
The examples count caryopses or grains per spikelet or flower. That is a count of another part, not an amount of the caryopsis itself.

Leaf width is meaningful. 'Increased width' is a value, but most examples are measurements, which should go to the width attribute. A rule would need to send measured widths to PATO width and keep only 'wide' for this value.
The examples are rhizome scales and a leaf shape (deltoid), not trichomes. Triangular trichomes are not a usual character.
Wrong bearer. The examples describe the hairiness of the shoot axis ('central region glabrous or bearing hairs'), not of a trichome.
Wrong bearer. 'Central region glabrous' is about the axis or region. A trichome cannot be glabrous.
Sori can be crowded or closely packed.
Teeth can be prominent.
The lodicule (squamella) margin or apex can be erose. The examples are correct.
The perigynium base or orifice can be truncate. Some examples describe the beak, which is a sub-part.

A rough lemma is meaningful. The examples are a 'fruiting scale' (a sedge part) read as a fertile lemma. A rule would need to map 'fruiting scale' to the sedge scale or perigynium, and not to the lemma.
Spines and thorns can be blunt.
Seed cones can be globose. One example, 'apex round', is a different shape.
Inflorescence branches and rachillae can be pendulous or nodding.
A perianth tube can be campanulate.
Achenes can be exserted from the disc or involucre.
Achenes can be grooved or have a dorsal groove.
The examples are about the beak, angles and midnerves, which are other parts. The achene itself is not described as obscure.
Achenes can be woolly.
Corona lobes can be incurved over the style apex.
A style can be pale or pallid. This is a pale colour, which low saturation approximates.

Distichous describes how leaves are arranged on the shoot (leaf arrangement), not the blade. A rule would need to send 'blades distichous' to the leaf or shoot, and keep it on the lamina only for equitant leaves.
The achene base can be cuneate.
Corolla lobes or the limb can be ascending.
Seeds can be light-coloured or pale.
An organ apex can be obtuse or rounded.
Bracts can be hidden by other parts or by perigynia.
The PATO term means an edge that can cut. The examples describe a sharply pointed apex, which is acute or pointed.
The examples describe the midnerves (veins) of the bract, not the bract. The vein is the bearer.
A cypsela can have a colour. The examples describe the apical collar, a sub-part. A rule would need to give the collar its own bearer or mark it as a part of the cypsela.
Sepals can be cup-shaped or cupped.
The examples are protuberances of a disc, not of the corolla lip. The bearer is wrong.
Bark can be checkered or tessellated.
Sepals or sepal margins can be incised or cut. The examples are correct.
'Paired' is the arrangement of teeth along the margin, not a quality of one tooth. A rule would need to send tooth arrangement to the margin or lamina. 'Gland-dotted' is a different quality.
Hydathodes can be superficial or sunken.
The hypanthium can be setose.
A tubercle has a diameter. The examples are measurements.
The corona can be united to the column or the corolla. The examples are correct.
The examples are about trichomes, not the whole plant. The bearer is wrong.
A cincinnus is coiled (circinate).
Leaves can be fragrant or malodorous.
Trichomes can be unicellular.
Bracts or their margins can be cartilaginous.
Leaf veins can be hairy (strigose, pilose).
The examples are cypselae (fruits), not seeds. The bearer is wrong.
Seeds can be flattened dorsiventrally.
A corolla plica margin or summit can be erose.
'Wider' is a comparison between parts (lateral and dorsal sepals), not a quality of one sepal. Pattern 10 or a comparison rule should handle it.
The shape of a staminal tube is meaningful. The examples are mixed: column, margin and corolla shapes. A rule would need to assign each phrase to the right part first.
Lobes can themselves be pinnately divided.
The examples are glands, a cyme and an age effect, not the whole plant. The bearer is wrong.
Tepals can have a colour such as straw.
A stem base can be terete.
Teeth can be antrorse.
Trichomes can have a bulbous base or tip.
The PATO term means compact or condensed. The examples mean flattened ('compressed laterally'), which is a different quality.
Bracteoles or their margins can be dissected or divided.
Scale leaves and their margins can be hairy.
